extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Aristotle; learners of moral philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and interpretation of Aristotle's account of Justice, Equity, Voluntariness, and the intellectual virtues (Knowledge, Art, Practical Wisdom, Science, Intuition) as presented in Books V–VI of the Nicomachean Ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'being unjustly dealt with'
rubrics_metrics.description: Being unjustly dealt with requires hurting a person with knowledge of the person hurt, the instrument and the manner of hurting him, and the fact of its being against the wish of the man who is hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hurt is with the person's consent (even through weakness of self-control) it is not 'being unjustly dealt with'; voluntariness and being against the victim's wish are essential. Examples: giving away one's own property willingly is not being unjustly dealt with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness as condition of unjust action
rubrics_metrics.description: An unjust action must be voluntary: done with knowledge (to whom and wherewith) and with deliberate purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts done contrary to a person's true wish (e.g., from lack of self-control) or done in ignorance are not unjust in the same sense. Voluntariness attaches to the originator of the action (the distributor rather than the receiver).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origination determines who acts unjustly in distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of unequal distribution, the distributor (the originator of the act) is the one who acts unjustly, not the person who happens to receive the larger share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntariness and the 'doing' attach to the party from whom the action originates. An erroneous award made in ignorance is not legally unjust though it may be morally problematic; knowingly wrong adjudication counts as unjust and benefits the wrongdoer similarly to receiving material unjust gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice implies plurality of persons (cannot unjustly deal solely with oneself)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man cannot, strictly speaking, deal unjustly by himself because justice/unjustice presuppose relations between multiple persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: unjust action must be voluntary and aggressive toward another; one cannot be unjustly dealt with with one's own consent; crimes (seducing one's own wife, stealing one's own property) are impossible against oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressiveness/hostility required for unjust action (not mere requital)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unjust action is not mere retaliation; it must be aggressive. One who hurts only in requital for prior hurt is not thought to act unjustly in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unjust action must be deliberate and aggressive rather than a symmetric requital; this distinguishes wrongful aggression from permitted retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice requires appropriate inward dispositions, not only external acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtue (including justice) is determined by inward dispositions and the right manner of performing actions, not merely by performing the outward deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely having the capacity to do unjust or brave acts is not sufficient to be unjust or brave; the inward state that accompanies action (the right dispositions) is crucial. Analogies: medicine—not merely using a knife but using it correctly for health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity defined as correction of law's universality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Equitable is Just, but better than that form of Just which is in accordance with written law; equity is 'a correction of law, where law is defective by reason of its universality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because laws state universal rules and cannot cover every particular exception, equity supplies the correction a lawgiver would have made had they foreseen the specific case. Thus equitable judgments waive strict legal letter when universality causes unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the Equitable man
rubrics_metrics.description: The Equitable man tends to choose and carry out equitable principles, and refrains from pressing the letter of the law on the worse side; he waives strict legal claims though backed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity is a species of Justice (not a different moral state) and is praiseworthy because it corrects unjust results produced by universal laws in particular situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between forms of Justice (law-enforced vs. natural/abstract)
rubrics_metrics.description: One class of Just is that enforced by law according to Virtue in its most extensive sense; law covers general cases while natural or abstract justice may differ from legal justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal justice may be 'right' in law but not coincide with primary or natural justice; ignorance can affect legal culpability though not necessarily the abstract justness of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean determined by Right Reason for moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Each moral virtue is a mean between excess and defect, and this mean is determined according to the dictates of Right Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying 'choose the mean' is insufficient without defining what Right Reason is; the mean must be specified relative to the work or function of the virtue (analogy to physician's application of medicine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the Rational Soul: calculative and non-calculative parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rational part of the soul divides into two: one apt to know (that which apprehends necessary truths) and one apt to calculate (the calculative or deliberative faculty concerned with things that can be otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division grounds further distinctions among intellectual virtues and explains why deliberation concerns contingent matters while certain truths are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three functions underlying moral action: Sense, Intellect, Appetition (Will)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral action and truth depend on Sense, Intellect, and Appetition (vague desire or definite Will); Sense does not originate moral action, whereas Intellect and Will are connected: what Intellect affirms the Will must pursue for right moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral Choice arises from deliberation (Intellect) causing Will; moral action requires both correct intellectual operation and proper moral character—truth of reason and rightness of will are jointly required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge (episteme) as demonstrative, necessary, teachable
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is 'a state or mental faculty apt to demonstrate syllogistically'; its objects are necessary/eternal, and it is capable of being taught (induction provides universals, syllogism reasons from them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge concerns things that cannot be otherwise and depends on demonstrative reasoning from first principles established by induction; knowledge differs from opinion and is not about contingent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (techne) as true reason apt to make
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is 'a state of mind, conjoined with true Reason, apt to Make' and concerns production/contrivance of contingent, non-natural things; its absence is the state conjoined with false Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art deals with what the maker originates and is concerned with making (contingent) rather than doing; art admits of degrees and can be judged by skill and accuracy in production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) defined and its domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom is 'a state of mind true, conjoined with Reason, and apt to Do, having for its object those things which are good or bad for Man'—the capacity to deliberate well about living well when no definite rule exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical Wisdom is distinct from Knowledge and Art: it concerns contingent human matters and action; it requires acquaintance with particulars as well as principles, is aimed at human good, and is not an art (it does not admit degrees in the same way). It is the virtue that preserves correct notion of one's true interest against corruption by pleasure or pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom requires knowledge of particulars as well as principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Practical Wisdom is 'apt to act,' it is necessary to know particular details, not merely general principles; particulars often matter more for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience-based particulars can make someone more practically wise than one with only abstract knowledge; practical wisdom includes supreme and subordinate forms depending on scope of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as union of Knowledge and Intuition; highest form of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is the most accurate kind of Knowledge, combining Knowledge and Intuition (the faculty taking in first principles); its objects are the most precious and eternal things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science in this sense is different from Practical Wisdom: it is universal and necessary, not varied by human concerns; it presupposes possession of truth about first principles and deductive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in evaluative standards between Art and Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Art admits degrees of excellence and a purposely wrong artist is sometimes preferable to an unwittingly wrong one; Practical Wisdom does not admit such degrees and is not assessed the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction informs judgment: methodological errors in art can be ranked, but in practical wisdom moral fault is not mitigated by purposefulness in the same beneficial manner.
